facts.fact: Widely cited win-back benchmarks, as summarized by SendPulse, place recovered inactive subscribers at about 5 to 15%, with stronger programs reaching 10 to 20% or more.
facts.quote: Widely cited win-back benchmarks place recovered inactive subscribers at about **5 to 15%**, with stronger programs reaching **10 to 20% or more**

facts.fact: Practical guidance commonly places the inactivity trigger for a re-engagement segment between three and six months, depending on send frequency.
facts.quote: Practical guidance commonly places the trigger somewhere between **three and six months**, depending on send frequency

facts.fact: One deliverability guide recommends enrolling contacts in a reactivation flow after more than four months without an open.
facts.quote: one deliverability guide recommends enrolling contacts after more than **four months** without an open

facts.fact: The page defines a cool dormant segment as contacts quiet for 60 to 120 days, and a cold segment as contacts inactive for 120 days or longer.
facts.quote: A cool contact might have gone quiet for **60 to 120 days**, while a cold contact has been inactive for **120 days or longer**.

facts.fact: The page recommends sending the first reactivation email on day 0 and the second diagnostic email around day 7 to non-reactivated subscribers.
facts.quote: Send the first message on day 0.

facts.fact: The page's diagram of subscriber attrition, dropping monthly active subscribers from 40% to 18% over two quarters, is explicitly hypothetical and not a reported business result.
facts.unit: % monthly active subscribers over two quarters
facts.quote: The graphic below illustrates a hypothetical active-subscriber decline, not a reported business result.

facts.fact: MailGenius guidance recommends a clear sunset rule that moves non-responders to inactive status after the reactivation sequence.
facts.quote: Guidance from [MailGenius on win-back campaigns](https://www.mailgenius.com/win-back-campaign/) recommends a clear sunset rule and moving non-responders to inactive status after the sequence.

facts.fact: The page recommends sending the final reactivation message around day 14 of the sequence.
facts.quote: Send the final message around day 14. Now you can introduce a concrete incentive, a specific deadline, or a final preference choice.

facts.fact: The page states that a structured reactivation sequence can run for roughly 30 days, with early messages separated by 5 to 7 days.
facts.value: 30 days; 5 to 7 days between early messages
facts.quote: A structured sequence can run for roughly **30 days**, with early messages separated by **5 to 7 days**, followed by a final notice before inactive contacts are archived.

facts.fact: The page attributes its reactivation timing guidance (the sequence length and spacing) to SendPulse's re-engagement sequence recommendations.
facts.quote: See [SendPulse’s re-engagement sequence recommendations](https://sendpulse.com/blog/re-engagement-email) for timing guidance.

facts.fact: The page recommends reporting reactivation campaign results on a 30-day reporting cadence.
facts.quote: Report results on a **30-day reporting cadence**, then decide whether each segment returns to regular messaging, enters a quarterly win-back cycle, or remains suppressed.

facts.fact: The page recommends moving non-responders to suppression or a low-frequency inactive list after the third reactivation email.
facts.quote: After the third email, move non-responders to suppression or a low-frequency inactive list.

facts.fact: The page recommends that the sequence stop as soon as a contact opens, clicks meaningfully, purchases, replies, updates preferences, unsubscribes, or reaches a suppression condition.
facts.quote: The sequence should stop as soon as someone opens, clicks meaningfully, purchases, replies, or updates preferences.

facts.fact: The page recommends including a one-click unsubscribe and a preference-center link in the final reactivation email.
facts.quote: Include a one-click unsubscribe and a preference-center link.

facts.fact: The page recommends verifying SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication before launching a reactivation campaign.
facts.quote: Verify **SPF, DKIM, and DMARC**, review blacklist status, and run seed tests across the inboxes customers use.

facts.fact: The page recommends sending to a large dormant segment in controlled batches rather than releasing the whole audience at once.
facts.quote: Send to a large dormant segment in controlled batches rather than releasing the whole audience at once.

facts.fact: The page recommends that a sunset policy move the sequence's non-responders to suppression, and it cites a 30-day reporting cadence as part of the post-campaign review.
facts.quote: Report results on a **30-day reporting cadence**

facts.fact: The page states that the first reactivation email generally gives the clearest signal, while later touches often deliver diminishing returns.
facts.quote: The first email generally gives the clearest signal, while later touches often deliver diminishing returns.

facts.fact: The page recommends excluding recent buyers and recently reactivated contacts from win-back campaigns, citing the MailGenius win-back checklist.
facts.quote: excluding recent buyers or recently reactivated contacts

facts.fact: The page describes a 30-day reactivation rollout for email campaigns.
facts.quote: A workable 30-day rollout

facts.fact: The page recommends a reactivation email flow of three emails, ordered as value first, feedback second, and urgency last.
facts.quote: Launch the three-email flow with value first, feedback second, and urgency last.

facts.fact: The page lays out the reactivation rollout in four weekly phases: diagnosis, delivery, amplification, and decisions.
facts.quote: Week four is for decisions.

facts.fact: The page says the reactivation workflow should be stopped for any subscriber who reactivates.
facts.quote: stop the workflow for anyone who reactivates
